candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls HTTP request parameter names (e.g., sending `%C4%B0d=...` in a form POST or query string). Parameter names are delivered unchanged to `DataBinder.checkAllowedFields` via `ServletRequestParameterPropertyValues` / `ServletRequestDataBinder.bind(ServletRequest)` (spring-web lines 153-170); they are not normalized before the deny-list check. The attacker only needs the target property name (e.g., `id`, `isAdmin`) to begin with a lowercase-'i' ASCII sequence that the application protected with `setDisallowedFields`.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked whether the field name is normalized before the deny-list check (it is not; raw parameter names reach checkAllowedFields via ServletRequestParameterPropertyValues). Checked whether property resolution is wholly case-insensitive (it is not, only the first-character uncapitalize/capitalize fallback exists), so the two transformations genuinely diverge. Verified `StringUtils.uncapitalize` uses single-char `Character.toLowerCase` and `setDisallowedFields` lowercases patterns with `toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)`. Also considered that `PatternMatchUtils.simpleMatchIgnoreCase` may be an unrelated public utility addition rather than a reverted fix call site; the finding does not depend on that inference. No tests exist in the snapshot to confirm intended semantics, and no code was executed.
candidates.impact: Bypass of the `disallowedFields` deny-list, i.e., of the documented mass-assignment/field-level protection: request data can modify object properties the application explicitly excluded from binding. Depending on the target property (identifiers such as `id`, internal flags such as `isAdmin`/`isInternal`), this enables data tampering or privilege/state manipulation. Integrity impact; attacker-controlled data reaches protected setters.
candidates.prerequisites: 1) A Spring MVC/WebFlux (or manual) application that relies on `DataBinder`/`WebDataBinder.setDisallowedFields(...)` for mass-assignment/field protection (the documented security use). 2) The protected target property begins with ASCII lowercase 'i' (e.g., `id`, `isAdmin`). 3) The attacker can submit a parameter whose name is 'İ' (U+0130) followed by the rest of the property name; the container must pass the UTF-8-decoded non-ASCII name through (standard). 4) JDK behavior: `String.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)` applies the full Unicode special mapping U+0130 -> U+0069 U+0307, while `Character.toLowerCase(U+0130)` (used by the binding fallback) yields U+0069.
candidates.root_cause: `DataBinder.isAllowed()` (spring-context/.../DataBinder.java:1158-1163) decides whether a field may be bound by lowercasing the attacker-controllable field name with `String.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)` and matching it against lowercased disallowed patterns (see `setDisallowedFields`, lines 565-576). That full Unicode lowercase mapping changes U+0130 'İ' into the two-code-point string "i̇", so "İd" becomes "i̇d" and no longer equals/matches a disallowed pattern such as "id". Bean-property resolution, however, uses a lenient fallback in `CachedIntrospectionResults.getPropertyDescriptor()` (spring-beans/.../CachedIntrospectionResults.java:380-391) that retries with `StringUtils.uncapitalize(name)`, and `StringUtils.changeFirstCharacterCase` (spring-core/.../StringUtils.java:587-605) uses single-character `Character.toLowerCase`, which maps 'İ' to plain 'i', yielding "id". The two different case transformations are applied to the same security check vs. the same binding decision, so a value can fail the deny-list but still resolve to the protected property.
candidates.title: DataBinder disallowedFields deny-list bypass via Unicode lowercasing mismatch (U+0130 'İ')
candidates.trace: Request parameter "İd" -> ServiceRequestDataBinder/WebDataBinder.bind -> DataBinder.doBind -> checkAllowedFields (DataBinder.java:1124-1137): canonicalPropertyName("İd") = "İd"; isAllowed("İd") (1158-1163): "İd".toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT) = "i̇d" != "id" -> simpleMatch returns false -> property value is NOT removed; applyPropertyValues -> BeanWrapperImpl.getLocalPropertyHandler("İd") -> CachedIntrospectionResults.getPropertyDescriptor("İd") (380-391): exact lookup misses, uncapitalize("İd") (StringUtils 587-605) = 'i' + "d" = "id" -> property descriptor found -> protected property `id` is set from the attacker value despite being in `disallowedFields`.
candidates.unverified: Runtime confirmation was not possible (no execution permitted): the exact JVM case-mapping behavior (U+0130 full vs. simple mapping) and end-to-end binding are reasoned from documented Java semantics and source, not executed. It is also not verifiable from this snapshot alone whether `PatternMatchUtils.simpleMatchIgnoreCase` was intended as the replacement used by `DataBinder.isAllowed` upstream or whether some other fix site was removed. Other modules were only sampled, not exhaustively reviewed.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-178 Improper Handling of Case Sensitivity (mass-assignment deny-list bypass)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 4,767 repository files, all files visible subject to the tool's binary-file filter (NUL-byte files skipped) and a 5 MiB per-file text limit; no sensitive-name or symlink exclusions. The snapshot contains main and jmh sources only (test directories are absent), so no test-based verification was possible. P1 relation index: partial index (4,765 of 4,767 files indexed, 2 files missing), 59,845 symbols / 114,532 call edges / 932 facts; capabilities explicitly exclude semantic resolution, data flow and control flow, so all index output was treated as navigation hints and every cited location was verified against source text. Reviewed in depth: spring-context DataBinder/validation machinery, spring-web ServletRequestDataBinder/WebDataBinder/ContentDisposition/UriComponentsBuilder, spring-beans CachedIntrospectionResults/PropertyAccessorUtils/BeanWrapperImpl, spring-core StringUtils/PatternMatchUtils, spring-webmvc & spring-webflux resource resolution and functional resource lookup, spring-oxm XML hardening. Other modules were sampled only; coverage is not exhaustive.
limitations: No tests or build were run and no runtime behavior was observed; findings are static source-evidence leads only.
The P1 index has no data-flow/control-flow or semantic resolution, and 2 source files are missing from it; unreported code areas were not assumed reviewed.
Test sources are absent from the snapshot, so intended security semantics could not be cross-checked against unit tests.
The exploitability of the DataBinder finding depends on documented JDK Unicode case-mapping behavior that was reasoned about, not executed or reproduced.

summary: Spring Framework 6.1.20-SNAPSHOT snapshot (4,767 files; test sources are not present, only main/jmh). Static review focused on data binding, request/path handling and resource resolution, XML parsing, and URL parsing. Strongest lead: `DataBinder`'s `disallowedFields` deny-list (mass-assignment protection) is evaluated by lowercasing the attacker-supplied field name with `String.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)`, while property binding resolves names via a lenient `StringUtils.uncapitalize` fallback that uses single-character `Character.toLowerCase`. Because U+0130 ('İ') lowercases to the two-code-point sequence "i" + U+0307 under full Unicode lowercasing but to plain "i" under `Character.toLowerCase`, a parameter named "İd" (UTF-8 %C4%B0d) is not matched/removed by `isAllowed("id")` yet still binds to the protected `id` property. Notably, `PatternMatchUtils.simpleMatchIgnoreCase` (@since 6.1.20) exists but has no callers anywhere in the snapshot, which is consistent with removal/reversion of the case-insensitive matching that would close this gap. No other issue with comparable source evidence was found; the resource-path-traversal and XXE hardenings inspected appear intact.
